Add two plugins and a Lit panel appears inside Vite DevTools with a timeline, a
component tree and an update explainer. Dev-only and off by default.

<Aside type="tip" title="Not on Vite, or inspecting production?">
  The Lit Inspector extension puts the same panel in Chrome and Firefox DevTools
  for any site. See [Inspect any site with Lit
  Inspector](/guides/devtools/browser-extension/).
</Aside>

## Install `@vitejs/devtools`

Vite DevTools is the browser overlay from `@vitejs/devtools` that hosts plugin
panels. The Lit panel is one of those panels, so the overlay has to be there
first.

```sh frame="terminal"
npm install -D @vitejs/devtools
```

## Enable the panel

`timeline: true` injects the recording runtime into the page. `DevTools()`
provides the host the panel docks into. You need both.

```ts title="vite.config.ts"
import {defineConfig} from 'vite';
import {litPlugin} from '@oddsquad/vite-plugin-lit';
import {DevTools} from '@vitejs/devtools';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [litPlugin({timeline: true, sourceOverlay: true}), DevTools()],
});
```

`sourceOverlay: true` is optional. The Components tab needs it to pick an
element by pointing at it on the page.

Prefer to leave the config alone? Both options also read from the environment,
so a personal `.env.local` works just as well.

```ini title=".env.local"
LIT_PLUGIN_TIMELINE=true
LIT_PLUGIN_SOURCE_OVERLAY=true
```

<Aside type="caution" title="Experimental">
  `timeline` defaults to `false` while the panel is experimental. Everything it
  adds is dev-only and never reaches a production build. To inspect a production
  build anyway, see [Production builds](/reference/cli/#production-builds), and
  [DevTools features by host](/reference/devtools-hosts/) for what works there.
</Aside>

## Without Vite DevTools

<Since v="0.19.0" />

With `timeline: true` and no `DevTools()`, the dev server serves the panel on
its own at `/__lit/`, and prints the address under the ones Vite prints:

```text frame="terminal"
  ➜  Local:   http://localhost:5173/
  ➜  Lit DevTools: http://localhost:5173/__lit/
```

Open it in a tab next to the app. The first time, it asks for a one-time code
that the dev server prints in the terminal, the same check Vite DevTools makes
before its overlay connects; the browser remembers it after that. Set
`VITE_DEVTOOLS_DISABLE_CLIENT_AUTH=true` to skip the check on a machine only
you can reach. Everything else in this guide works the same, except that there
is no dock to bring forward: a pick on the page selects the element in the
open panel, but the panel's tab stays where it is.

## In a server that is not Vite

<Since v="0.22.0" />

A server without Vite can host the panel itself, on its own origin, without
the `lit-devtools dev` process. `createLitDevtools()` returns one web-standard
request handler for the panel, the page script and the RPC; mount it on a
catch-all route and load the script first in each page's `<head>`:

```ts
import {createLitDevtools} from '@oddsquad/vite-plugin-lit/devframe';
import {Elysia} from 'elysia';

const devtools = createLitDevtools();

new Elysia()
  .all(`${devtools.base}*`, ({request}) => devtools.handler(request))
  .get('/', () => page(`<script src="${devtools.script}"></script>`))
  .listen({hostname: 'localhost', port: 3000});
```

The handler takes a `Request` and returns a `Response`, so the same two lines
fit Hono, `Bun.serve`, a SvelteKit `+server.ts` or a Next.js route handler.

The panel is docked in the page: a Lit button in the bottom-right corner opens
it in a drawer along the bottom, which you can drag taller, and picking an
element opens it there. The page remembers whether the drawer was open and how
tall. It is also its own page at `/__lit-devtools/`; pass `base` to move it,
or `dock: false` to leave the page alone.

- **Auth.** On by default: the page asks for a one-time code that the server
  prints, once per browser. In a frame, such as a cloud IDE's preview, the
  browser cannot prompt, so the dock asks instead: its button carries a dot,
  and the drawer holds a field for the code. `createLitDevtools({auth: false})`
  skips the code; only do that on a server bound to loopback, since the RPC
  can open files in your editor.
- **Transport.** The RPC runs over a WebSocket that devframe serves on a spare
  local port of its own, so the host needs no upgrade wiring. The browser
  dials it on the page's hostname: pass `host: '127.0.0.1'` if your pages are
  on `127.0.0.1` rather than `localhost`. Behind a proxy or tunnel that
  exposes one port only, pass `transport: 'sse'` to keep the RPC on the
  host's origin. Over HTTP/1.1 each SSE stream holds one of the browser's six
  connections per host, and a docked page holds two, so stay at two tabs or
  serve over HTTP/2.
- **Cloud previews and tunnels.** Only loopback pages may connect by default.
  Name the others in `allowedOrigins`; a `*` in the host stands for any
  subdomain, so `['https://*.csb.app']` admits every CodeSandbox preview. Keep
  `auth` on there: the preview is reachable by more than your machine.
- **Limits.** As with `lit-devtools dev`: the tree, inspector and timeline
  work, component locations come from the page's sourcemaps, and HMR patching
  needs Vite. The [Elysia example](https://github.com/oddcelot/vite-plugin-lit/tree/main/examples/elysia)
  runs it this way.

## Open it and record ten seconds

Start the dev server, open the page, and open the Vite DevTools overlay. Lit
appears in the dock list with its own icon. The panel follows one page at a
time: opening the app in a second tab switches to that tab and says so.

<ThemedImage
  light={devtoolsPanelDockedLight}
  dark={devtoolsPanelDockedDark}
  alt="The Lit panel docked inside Vite DevTools, showing the Components tab."
/>

The panel opens on **Components** and carries four tabs.

- **Components** lists every Lit element on the page with its reactive state,
  and needs no recording. See
  [Inspect live components](/guides/devtools/components/).
- **Updates** answers which component re-rendered, how often, and why. See
  [Find out why a component re-rendered](/guides/devtools/updates/).
- **Timeline** records lifecycle, render and input events in order. Press
  **▶ Record**, click around for ten seconds, then press **⏹ Stop**. See
  [Record and read the timeline](/guides/devtools/timeline/).
- **Settings** shows the resolved configuration and overrides part of it live.

## Change settings live

The **Settings** tab shows what the plugin actually resolved: `litPlugin()`
options on top of `LIT_PLUGIN_*` environment variables on top of the defaults.

<ThemedImage
  light={devtoolsSettingsTabLight}
  dark={devtoolsSettingsTabDark}
  alt="The Settings tab listing the resolved options, with switches and menus for the ones that can be overridden live."
/>

The HMR behaviour, the source-overlay editor and the Components tab's own
toggles are editable there. A change reaches the running page at once, with no
dev-server restart and no edit to `vite.config.ts`. **Reset overrides** drops your
overrides and puts the resolved values back.

A value you set carries its origin in parentheses: `(option)` for
`litPlugin()`, `(env)` for a `LIT_PLUGIN_*` variable. So `Zed (env)` means the
editor came from your `.env`. A value with neither is the built-in default.
The same goes for each section's enabled or disabled pill, so `HMR disabled
(option)` means `litPlugin({hmr: false})` turned it off. Open a dropdown and the configured choice says where it came from, `default`
included. When env or an option set it, the built-in default is tagged
`default` too, so `warn env` sits beside `reload default`. Hovering a
setting's name explains it and gives its default.
An overridden row names
the value it replaced, such as `env: Zed`, and the small **×** beside it
resets just that row. A custom editor object from `litPlugin()`
shows as `Custom (option)` and can't be switched from the panel.

If the value underneath an override has changed since you made it, say you
switched the editor to Cursor and `.env` now says Zed, the row adds a line:
`Config changed since you overrode this: was VS Code, now Zed`. **Reset** drops
the override so the new value applies. **Keep** leaves it in place and stops
the reminder until the config changes again. Overrides saved before this
existed have nothing to compare against, so they never show it.

A setting whose feature is off at config time stays read-only. Its runtime was
never injected into the page, so there is nothing there to change.

Your overrides and the panel's light/dark choice persist per developer and
never touch the repository;
[DevTools architecture](/concepts/devtools-architecture/)
explains where they live and why there are two copies.
